concepts.label: MNCs and Production Across Countries
concepts.cardText: Until the middle of the twentieth century, production was largely organised within countries, and trade was the main channel connecting them. A multinational corporation (MNC) is a company that owns or controls production in more than one nation. MNCs set up offices and factories where they can get cheap labour and other resources, so that the cost of production is low and they earn greater profits. For example, an MNC may design products in the US, make components in China, assemble them in Mexico and Eastern Europe, and run customer care from call centres in India. The production process is divided into small parts and spread across the globe.

concepts.label: How MNCs Interlink Production
concepts.cardText: MNCs set up production close to markets, where labour is available at low cost and other factors of production are assured. Money spent on assets like land, buildings and machines is investment; investment by MNCs is foreign investment. MNCs may set up production jointly with local companies, bringing money and the latest technology. The most common route is to buy up local companies, as Cargill Foods bought Parakh Foods. MNCs also place orders with small producers, in garments, footwear and sports items, and sell under their own brands, with great power over price, quality, delivery and labour conditions. As a result, production in distant locations is getting interlinked.

concepts.topicTitle: Foreign trade and integration of markets
concepts.label: Foreign Trade and Integration of Markets
concepts.cardText: Foreign trade creates an opportunity for producers to reach beyond domestic markets, and for buyers to choose goods beyond what is produced at home. When Chinese toy makers export cheaper, new-design toys to India, 70 to 80 per cent of toy shops replace Indian toys within a year: Indian buyers get more choice at lower prices and Chinese makers expand, but Indian toy makers face losses. With trade, the choice of goods rises, prices of similar goods in the two markets tend to become equal, and producers in distant countries compete closely. Foreign trade thus integrates markets in different countries.

concepts.label: What Is Globalisation?
concepts.cardText: In the past two to three decades, more MNCs have looked for cheap locations, so foreign investment has been rising, and foreign trade has risen rapidly, with a large part controlled by MNCs. The result of greater foreign investment and greater foreign trade has been greater integration of production and markets across countries. Globalisation is this process of rapid integration or interconnection between countries, and MNCs are playing a major role in it. Goods, services, investments and technology move between countries, but movement of people has not increased much because of restrictions.

concepts.label: Technology and Globalisation
concepts.cardText: Rapid improvement in technology has been one major factor stimulating globalisation. Transport technology has made faster delivery of goods over long distances possible at lower costs: goods are placed in containers loaded intact onto ships, railways, planes and trucks, hugely reducing port handling costs, and air transport costs have fallen. Information and communication technology (telecommunications, computers, the Internet) has played a major role in spreading production of services across countries. For example, a news magazine for London readers is designed and printed in Delhi, with text, instructions and payment sent over the Internet.

concepts.label: Liberalisation of Foreign Trade and Investment
concepts.cardText: A tax on imports, like a tax on imported toys, is a trade barrier: a restriction governments use to regulate foreign trade. After Independence, India put barriers on foreign trade and investment to protect producers from foreign competition, since industries were just coming up in the 1950s and 1960s; only essential items like machinery, fertilisers and petroleum were imported. Around 1991, India decided its producers should compete globally, as competition would improve their performance and quality; this was supported by powerful international organisations. Removing barriers or restrictions set by the government is called liberalisation.

concepts.label: World Trade Organisation
concepts.cardText: The World Trade Organisation (WTO) aims to liberalise international trade. Started at the initiative of developed countries, it establishes rules for international trade and sees that they are obeyed; about 160 countries are members. In practice, developed countries have unfairly retained trade barriers, while WTO rules have forced developing countries to remove them. For example, US farmers, only 0.5 per cent of US employment, receive massive government support, so they sell farm products abroad at abnormally low prices, hurting farmers in other countries. Developing countries ask: is this free and fair trade?

concepts.label: Who Has Benefited from Globalisation?
concepts.cardText: Greater competition among local and foreign producers has benefited consumers, particularly the well-off in urban areas, who enjoy more choice, better quality and lower prices, and so higher standards of living. But among producers and workers, the impact has not been uniform. MNCs have increased investment in India in cell phones, automobiles, electronics, soft drinks, fast food and banking, creating new jobs and helping local suppliers. Several top Indian companies have benefited by investing in newer technology, and some, like Tata Motors, Infosys, Ranbaxy, Asian Paints and Sundaram Fasteners, have become multinationals. New opportunities have opened in IT-based services.

concepts.label: Steps to Attract Foreign Investment
concepts.cardText: Central and state governments take special steps to attract foreign companies. Special Economic Zones (SEZs) are set up with world-class facilities like electricity, water, roads, transport and storage, and companies there pay no taxes for an initial period of five years. The government has also allowed flexibility in labour laws: instead of hiring workers regularly, companies hire them 'flexibly' for short periods when work is intense, to reduce labour costs. Foreign companies are demanding even more flexibility.

concepts.label: Small Producers: Compete or Perish
concepts.cardText: For many small producers and workers, globalisation has posed major challenges. Ravi started a capacitor unit in Hosur in 1992; his struggle began when the government removed restrictions on imports of capacitors under its WTO agreement in 2001. Television companies moved to assembling for MNCs and preferred imports at half his price. Ravi now produces less than half of what he did in 2000 and has only seven workers. Batteries, capacitors, plastics, toys, tyres, dairy products and vegetable oil are industries where small manufacturers have been hit hard. Small and medium industries employ about 11 crore workers, next only to agriculture.

concepts.label: Competition and Uncertain Employment
concepts.cardText: Faced with growing competition, most employers now prefer to employ workers 'flexibly', so workers' jobs are no longer secure. Large garment MNCs in Europe and America look for the cheapest goods; to win orders, Indian exporters cut labour costs by hiring temporary workers, with long hours, night shifts and low wages. Sushila, once a permanent garment worker with health insurance and provident fund, is now a temporary worker earning less than half as much, with no benefits. While MNCs make large profits, workers are denied their fair share of the benefits of globalisation. Conditions in the organised sector have come to resemble the unorganised sector.

concepts.topicTitle: The struggle for a fair globalisation
concepts.label: The Struggle for a Fair Globalisation
concepts.cardText: Not everyone has benefited from globalisation: people with education, skill and wealth have made the best use of the new opportunities, while many have not shared the benefits. Fair globalisation would create opportunities for all and ensure that its benefits are shared better. The government can play a major role: ensuring labour laws are properly implemented and workers get their rights, supporting small producers until they can compete, using trade and investment barriers if necessary, negotiating at the WTO for 'fairer rules', and aligning with other developing countries. Campaigns by people's organisations have also influenced decisions at the WTO.
